2.THE EFFECT OF THE DUE PROCESS CLAUSE
Traditionally, a creditor who sued a debtor could invoke a provisional remedy to seize property of the debtor without affording the
property owner notice of the action or an opportunity to contest the underlying claim. See Chapter 3.D, supra. In a series of decisions
beginning in the 1960s, see p. 279, supra, the Supreme Court extended the protections of the Due Process Clause to the use of provisional
remedies, developing a flexible standard that considered the significance of the property at stake and the exigencies of the situation, such
as concerns of the debtor’s flight or that the property would be dissipated or concealed. See Countryman, The Bill of Rights and the Bill
Collector, 15 Ariz.L.Rev. 521 (1973).
A garnishment order directs a third party (the garnishee) that is holding money or property of the debtor to give the property instead
to the creditor-garnishor. In SNIADACH v. FAMILY FINANCE CORP., the Supreme Court invalidated the Wisconsin prejudgment
garnishment procedure, which authorized a summons to issue at the request of the creditor’s lawyer who served the garnishee—the
debtor’s employer who held wages lawfully due to the employee—thereby freezing the debtor’s wages during the period before trial of
the main suit. In FUENTES v. SHEVIN, the Court extended Sniadach’s reasoning to replevin, a procedure that at common law allowed
for the recovery of personal property claimed to have been unlawfully taken. In Fuentes, the Court invalidated as unconstitutional state
statutes authorizing the replevin of chattels—consumer goods sold on an installment contract—before allowing the debtor notice and an
opportunity to be heard. See Clark & Landers, Sniadach, Fuentes and Beyond: The Creditor Meets the Constitution, 59 Va.L.Rev. 355
(1973); Feeherry & Zuckerman, Note—Procedural Due Process—The Prior Hearing Rule and the Demise of Ex Parte Remedies, 53

B.U.L.Rev. 41 (1973).
The Court in MITCHELL v. W.T. GRANT CO. upheld the Louisiana sequestration statute, which permitted the creditor to obtain the
writ on an ex parte application without giving the debtor either notice or an opportunity for a hearing. The Court reasoned that the risk of
a wrongful taking was minimized by the creditor’s pre-existing interest in the property; the fact that a judge, and not a clerk, authorized
the writ; the immediate availability of a post-seizure hearing; and the risk that the debtor could conceal or destroy the property quickly
and easily, thus depriving the creditor of the security interest. However, in NORTH GEORGIA FINISHING, INC. v. DI-CHEM, INC.,
